title: Compound Interest
definition: Interest calculated on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. Often called the eighth wonder of the world.
formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)
example: Invest $1,000 at 8% annual interest compounded monthly for 10 years: A = 1000(1 + 0.08/12)^(12*10) = $2,219.64
key_stat: 8% over 30 years = 10x your money
why_it_matters: Starting early matters more than investing more later. A 25-year-old investing $200/month at 8% will have more at 65 than a 35-year-old investing $400/month.

title: P/E Ratio
definition: Price-to-Earnings ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of earnings. It's the stock price divided by earnings per share.
formula: P/E = Stock Price / EPS
example: A stock trading at $150 with EPS of $5 has a P/E of 30. Investors pay $30 for every $1 of earnings.
key_stat: S&P 500 avg P/E: ~20-25 historically
why_it_matters: A high P/E could mean overvaluation OR high growth expectations. Compare P/E within the same industry, not across sectors.

title: Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)
definition: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of market price. You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.
formula: Shares bought = Fixed Amount / Current Price
example: Investing $500/month: Month 1 at $50 = 10 shares, Month 2 at $40 = 12.5 shares, Month 3 at $60 = 8.33 shares. Average cost: $48.33/share vs avg price $50.
key_stat: Reduces avg cost by 5-15% in volatile markets
why_it_matters: Removes the need to time the market. Psychologically easier than lump-sum investing during downturns.

title: Rule of 72
definition: A quick shortcut to estimate how long it takes for an investment to double. Divide 72 by the annual return rate.
formula: Years to Double = 72 / Annual Return %
example: At 8% annual return: 72/8 = 9 years to double. At 12%: 72/12 = 6 years.
key_stat: At 7%: ~10 years to double
why_it_matters: Quick mental math for comparing investments. Helps set realistic expectations for long-term growth.

title: EMI (Equated Monthly Installment)
definition: A fixed monthly payment made by a borrower to a lender. Each payment covers both interest and principal repayment.
example: A $200,000 loan at 6% for 30 years: EMI = $1,199.10/month. Total payment: $431,676. Total interest: $231,676.
key_stat: At 6% over 30 years, you pay 116% of loan as interest
why_it_matters: Understanding EMI helps you evaluate whether to take a loan, compare lenders, and decide on tenure.

title: Position Sizing
definition: Determining how much capital to allocate to a single trade or investment. The 1-2% rule says never risk more than 1-2% of your total capital on one trade.
formula: Max Position = (Account Size * Risk %) / (Entry - Stop Loss)
example: Account: $50,000, Risk 2%, Entry: $100, Stop Loss: $95. Max position = ($50,000 * 0.02) / $5 = 200 shares.
key_stat: 2% rule: survive 10 consecutive losses and still have 82% capital
why_it_matters: Prevents catastrophic losses. A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to break even.

title: Inflation
definition: The rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises, eroding purchasing power over time.
formula: Real Return = Nominal Return - Inflation Rate
example: If your savings account earns 4% and inflation is 3%, your real return is only 1%.
key_stat: 3% inflation halves purchasing power in 24 years
why_it_matters: Cash loses value over time. Investments must beat inflation to grow real wealth.

title: Diversification
definition: Spreading investments across different asset classes, sectors, and geographies to reduce risk. Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
formula: Portfolio Risk < Weighted Avg of Individual Risks (when correlations < 1)
example: A portfolio of 60% stocks / 40% bonds had lower max drawdown (-35%) than 100% stocks (-50%) in 2008.
key_stat: 30 uncorrelated stocks eliminate ~90% of unsystematic risk
why_it_matters: The only free lunch in finance. Reduces risk without necessarily reducing expected returns.

title: Dividend Yield
definition: Annual dividends per share divided by the stock price. Measures the cash return from dividends alone.
formula: Dividend Yield = Annual Dividend / Stock Price
example: A stock at $100 paying $3/year in dividends has a 3% yield.
key_stat: S&P 500 avg yield: ~1.5-2%
why_it_matters: Dividend stocks provide income regardless of price movements. Reinvested dividends account for ~40% of total stock returns historically.

title: Market Capitalization
definition: Total market value of a company's outstanding shares. Calculated by multiplying share price by total shares outstanding.
formula: Market Cap = Share Price * Shares Outstanding
example: Apple with ~15.5 billion shares at $180 = $2.79 trillion market cap.
key_stat: Mega-cap: >$200B, Mid-cap: $10-200B, Small-cap: <$10B
why_it_matters: Determines company size classification, index inclusion, and risk profile. Larger caps tend to be more stable.

title: Volatility (VIX)
definition: A statistical measure of the dispersion of returns. The VIX measures expected 30-day volatility of the S&P 500 based on options prices.
formula: Standard Deviation of Returns * sqrt(252) for annualized
example: VIX at 15 = market expects ~15% annualized volatility. VIX above 30 = high fear.
key_stat: VIX historical avg: ~19. Above 30 = extreme fear.
why_it_matters: High volatility = higher risk AND higher potential returns. VIX spikes often mark market bottoms.

title: Opportunity Cost
definition: The value of the next best alternative you give up when making a choice. Every dollar invested in A is a dollar not invested in B.
formula: Opportunity Cost = Return of Best Foregone Option - Return of Chosen Option
example: Keeping $10,000 in a 4% savings account instead of an index fund returning 10% costs you $600/year.
key_stat: $10K in mattress vs 8% index fund: $46K lost over 30 years
why_it_matters: Cash drag is real. Understanding opportunity cost helps optimize capital allocation.

title: Sharpe Ratio
definition: Measures risk-adjusted return. How much excess return you get for each unit of risk taken.
formula: Sharpe = (Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Std Dev of Returns
example: Portfolio returns 12%, risk-free rate 4%, std dev 15%. Sharpe = (12-4)/15 = 0.53
key_stat: Sharpe > 1 is good, > 2 is excellent
why_it_matters: A high return with high volatility may be worse than moderate return with low volatility. Sharpe tells you which.

title: Bull vs Bear Market
definition: A bull market is when prices rise 20%+ from recent lows. A bear market is when prices fall 20%+ from recent highs.
formula: Bull: +20% from low. Bear: -20% from high.
example: S&P 500 went from 666 (Mar 2009) to 3,386 (Feb 2020) — a 409% bull run lasting 11 years.
key_stat: Avg bull market lasts 4.4 years, avg bear lasts 1.1 years
why_it_matters: Bulls historically last much longer than bears. Time in the market beats timing the market.

title: Liquidity
definition: How quickly an asset can be converted to cash without significantly affecting its price. Cash is the most liquid asset.
formula: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
example: Large-cap stocks like Apple are highly liquid (millions of shares daily). Real estate is illiquid (takes months to sell).
key_stat: Bid-ask spread < 0.1% = highly liquid
why_it_matters: Illiquid assets may need to be sold at a discount in emergencies. Liquidity premium compensates for this risk.

title: Diversification Ratio
definition: The weighted average volatility of individual assets divided by portfolio volatility. Measures how much diversification benefit you're getting.
formula: DR = Weighted Avg Individual Vol / Portfolio Vol
example: If individual assets avg 20% vol but portfolio is 14% vol, DR = 1.43. You've reduced risk by 30%.
key_stat: DR > 1 means diversification is working
why_it_matters: Just owning many assets doesn't mean you're diversified. Correlations matter.

title: Cost Averaging vs Lump Sum
definition: Lump sum investing puts all money in at once. Cost averaging spreads it over time. Historically, lump sum wins ~68% of the time because markets trend upward.
formula: Lump Sum wins when market goes up. DCA wins when market goes down initially.
example: $120K invested lump sum in Jan 2020 vs $10K/month. By Dec 2021, lump sum won by ~15%.
key_stat: Lump sum beats DCA 68% of the time (Vanguard study)
why_it_matters: DCA is psychologically easier but mathematically inferior most of the time. Know the trade-off.

title: Expense Ratio
definition: Annual fee charged by mutual funds and ETFs, expressed as a percentage of assets. Deducted from returns.
formula: Annual Fee = Expense Ratio * Assets Under Management
example: A 0.03% expense ratio on $100K costs $30/year. A 1% ratio costs $1,000/year.
key_stat: Over 30 years, 1% fee eats ~25% of your returns
why_it_matters: Fees are the single best predictor of future fund returns. Lower is almost always better for index funds.

title: Credit Score
definition: A numerical rating (300-850) representing your creditworthiness. Based on payment history, credit utilization, length of history, types of credit, and new inquiries.
formula: FICO: 35% payment history + 30% utilization + 15% history length + 10% types + 10% inquiries
example: Score of 750+ gets best rates. A 760 vs 660 score on a $300K mortgage = ~$50K difference in interest over 30 years.
key_stat: 750+ = excellent. Below 670 = subprime rates.
why_it_matters: Affects mortgage rates, insurance premiums, rental applications, and even job prospects.

title: 401(k) Match
definition: Free money from your employer. They match a percentage of your contributions up to a limit.
formula: Match = Your Contribution * Match % (up to employer cap)
example: Employer matches 50% up to 6% of salary. Salary $80K: contribute $4,800, employer adds $2,400. That's an instant 50% return.
key_stat: Not taking the match = leaving $2,000-5,000/year on the table
why_it_matters: Always contribute at least enough to get the full match. It's a guaranteed 50-100% return before any market gains.
